output.summary:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Caffeine and Migraine KEY FINDINGS:
1. CAFFEINE PARADOX: Low-dose caffeine (1 cup/day) can acutely relieve migraine; high daily intake (>400mg) is a migraine trigger and increases analgesic overuse headache risk
2. CAFFEINE WITHDRAWAL: Abrupt reduction in high caffeine intake causes rebound headaches; gradual taper recommended (25% reduction per week)
3. MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE: Using analgesics (including ibuprofen) >10-15 days/month can trigger chronic daily headache; assess frequency
4. RECOMMENDATION: patients on 3-4 cups of coffee daily are advised to taper to ~1 cup/day over 4 weeks, with consistent timing to avoid withdrawal
5. STRESS + SLEEP: Irregular sleep and PhD stress are known migraine triggers; sleep hygiene counseling essential CONCLUSION: Reduce caffeine to 1 cup/day gradually; regular sleep schedule; stress management strategies. Daily caffeine intake above approximately 400 mg is associated with increased migraine frequency; gradual reduction (rather than abrupt cessation) avoids caffeine-withdrawal headache; irregular sleep and psychological stress are recognised migraine triggers

TREATMENT OPTIONS FOR MIGRAINE WITH AURA ACUTE TREATMENT:
1. Sumatriptan 100 mg at headache onset — first choice (75% response rate); repeat after 2 hours if partial relief
2. Naproxen sodium 550 mg combination with sumatriptan improves outcome PREVENTIVE THERAPY (≥4 migraine days/month):
1. Topiramate 25-100 mg/day — first-line; 50% attack reduction in RCTs; side effects: cognitive, paresthesias, weight loss
2. Propranolol 40-120 mg/day — first-line; avoid in asthma
3. Amitriptyline 10-75 mg QHS — first-line if comorbid anxiety/depression
4. Valproate — effective but avoid in women of childbearing age
5. CGRP antibodies (erenumab 70mg SC monthly) — newer, well-tolerated; approved for episodic migraine CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan has an established evidence base as first-line acute therapy for migraine attacks; multiple first-line preventive agents with Level A evidence are available; selection depends on comorbidities and tolerability per individual clinical assessment. Sumatriptan first-line acute; topiramate or propranolol preventive; CGRP monoclonal antibodies alternative

DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW Sumatriptan + caffeine: No significant interaction. Caffeine can enhance triptan absorption (used in Cafergot preparation). However, chronic high caffeine can cause rebound; not recommended as regular combination. CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan safe. Reduce caffeine separately. No sumatriptan-caffeine interaction; address caffeine intake separately

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

differential.key_features: Visual aura is reproducible and stereotyped — this is migraine with aura, not migraine without aura
Aura duration 20-30 min is too long for seizure propagation; no impaired awareness
No papilledema, no diurnal pattern, no visual obscurations; normal exam
Severe unilateral throbbing with photophobia, phonophobia and nausea is migrainous, not tension-type

key_clinical_evidence: Classic visual aura (expanding fortification spectra) over 20-30 min is the most common form of migraine aura
Routine MRI not indicated when ICHD-3 criteria are met and exam is normal [AAN_2000]
Increasing frequency in a young patient warrants preventive consideration but not extra diagnostic testing

patient.history_present_illness:
A 24-year-old Chinese-American woman presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of recurrent headaches with visual phenomena that started at age 19. She reports that approximately 8-10 times per year, she experiences a small blind spot in the center of her vision that gradually expands over 20-25 minutes into a bright, shimmering, crescent-shaped arc that sweeps to the periphery and then disappears. Following the resolution of the visual phenomenon, she develops a moderate-to-severe unilateral throbbing headache (typically right-sided, 7/10 intensity) with nausea and sensitivity to light, lasting 4-8 hours. She has missed several days of university and now graduate school due to these headaches.

She notes a significant increase in attack frequency since starting her PhD program 6 months ago, attributing it to stress, irregular sleep, and frequent caffeine intake (3-4 cups coffee daily). Her mother and maternal grandmother both had migraines throughout their reproductive years. She takes over-the-counter ibuprofen which gives partial relief. She has not tried triptans. She is not on oral contraceptives. She had a normal physical examination with her university health provider 4 months ago. She denies any limb weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, or any episodes that differ from her typical pattern.
